rules.title: The Accusative Case, Articles
rules.explanation: German marks the direct object with the **accusative** case. Only the **masculine** article changes: **der** becomes **den**, and **ein** becomes **einen** (feminine, neuter and plural articles stay the same). Ask **wen oder was?** (whom or what?) to find the object. Example: Ich habe **einen** Bruder. Ich sehe **den** Mann.

context_dialogue.speaker: TOM
context_dialogue.text: Dort ist **der** Kellner. Ich sehe **den** Mann am Fenster.
context_dialogue.translation: There's the waiter. I see the man by the window.

context_dialogue.speaker: ANNA
context_dialogue.translation: Good. Do you have a pen?

noticing_prompts.q: Which article changes shape when the noun is the object, der or die?
What form does 'ein' take in the accusative for a masculine noun?

structured_input.question: Why is 'einen' used instead of 'ein'?
options: Because 'Bruder' is a masculine direct object (accusative)
structured_input.feedback: 'Bruder' is the object of 'haben', so the masculine article takes the accusative form 'einen'.

structured_input.question: Which is true for you? Choose the sentence that fits your family.
options: Ich habe keinen Bruder und keine Schwester.
structured_input.feedback: Each option uses the accusative object. Notice 'einen' (masculine) vs 'eine' (feminine, unchanged).

quiz.feedback_why: 'Mann' is the masculine direct object, so 'der' becomes 'den' in the accusative.
'Bruder' is the masculine object of 'haben', so 'ein' becomes 'einen'.

communicative_production.prompt: Write one sentence about something you have or see, using the accusative (e.g. Ich habe einen ... / Ich sehe den ...).
communicative_production.model: Ich sehe den Mann und einen Hund.
communicative_production.model_translation: I see the man and a dog.
communicative_production.hint: Only the masculine article changes: der → den, ein → einen.

rules.title: The Three Genders, der, die, das
rules.title_en: The Three Genders, der, die, das
rules.title_es: Los tres géneros, der, die, das
rules.explanation: Every German noun has one of **three** genders, shown by its article: masculine **der**, feminine **die**, and neuter **das**. The gender belongs to the word, so learn each noun with its article. Feminine job/role nouns often add **-in** (der Lehrer, die Lehrerin).

context_dialogue.speaker: LEA
context_dialogue.translation: The man and the woman are reading.

context_dialogue.speaker: LEA
context_dialogue.translation: My sister is the teacher here.

noticing_prompts.q: Which article goes with 'Kind', der, die or das?
How is the feminine of 'der Lehrer' formed?

structured_input.question: Why is the article 'das'?
structured_input.feedback: 'Kind' is neuter, so it takes the neuter article 'das'.

structured_input.question: Which sentence is true for you? Pick one.
structured_input.feedback: Each noun carries its gender: der Hund (m), die Katze (f), das Pferd (n).

communicative_production.prompt: Write a sentence naming a person or thing with its correct article (der / die / das).
communicative_production.hint: Learn every noun together with its article.

rules.title: Separable Verbs
rules.explanation: Many German verbs have a **separable prefix** (auf, an, ein, mit, aus…). In a main clause the prefix detaches and moves to the **end**: aufstehen becomes 'Ich **stehe** früh **auf**.' Ankommen becomes 'Ich **komme** morgen **an**.'

context_dialogue.speaker: BEN
context_dialogue.translation: I get up at seven o'clock.

noticing_prompts.q: Where does the prefix 'auf' go in the sentence?
What is the base verb of 'stehe ... auf'?

structured_input.question: Why is 'auf' at the end of the sentence?
options: Because 'aufstehen' is a separable verb and the prefix detaches
Because the sentence is a question
structured_input.feedback: 'aufstehen' is separable, so in a main clause the prefix 'auf' moves to the end.

structured_input.question: Which describes your morning? Choose the true one.
options: Am Wochenende stehe ich sehr spät auf.
structured_input.feedback: In each one the prefix 'auf' jumps to the end: aufstehen → stehe ... auf.

quiz.translation: I get up at seven o'clock.
quiz.feedback_why: The separable prefix of 'aufstehen' goes to the end.
The separable prefix of 'ankommen' goes to the end.

communicative_production.prompt: Write a sentence with a separable verb (aufstehen, ankommen, einkaufen ...) about your day.
communicative_production.hint: The prefix moves to the end: einkaufen → kaufe ... ein.
